claims.quote: As a matter of fact, as the American reader at least will promptly see, the much more practicable thing is that upper footpath, with these moving platforms beside it, running out over the street after the manner of the viaduct of an elevated railroad.
claims.description: Raised footpaths with moving walkway platforms beside them run above city streets like an elevated railway.

claims.quote: Will this diversion of the vast omnibus traffic of to-day into the air and underground, together with the segregation of van traffic to specific routes and times, be the only change in the streets of the new century?
claims.description: City bus traffic is moved onto elevated and underground ways, and freight vans are restricted to set routes and hours.

claims.quote: I do not see what is to prevent the process of elimination that is beginning now with the heavy vans spreading until it covers all horse traffic
claims.description: Horse-drawn traffic will disappear from city streets entirely.

claims.quote: with the disappearance of horse hoofs and the necessary filth of horses, the road surface may be made a very different thing from what it is at present, better drained and admirably adapted for the soft-tired hackney vehicles and the torrent of cyclists
claims.description: Once horses are gone, roads can be rebuilt with better drainage and surfaces suited to rubber-tired vehicles and bicycles.

claims.quote: Moreover, there will be little to prevent a widening of the existing side walks, and the protection of the passengers from rain and hot sun by awnings, or such arcades as distinguish Turin, or Sir F. Bramwell's upper footpaths on the model of the Chester rows.
claims.description: Sidewalks are widened and sheltered from rain and sun by awnings, arcades or raised covered footpaths.

claims.quote: Moreover, there is no reason but the existing filth why the roadways should not have translucent *velaria* to pull over in bright sunshine and wet weather.
claims.description: Retractable translucent awnings can be pulled over entire roadways in strong sun or rain.

claims.quote: an easily portable substance, which could be decomposed electrically by wind or water power, and which would then recombine and supply force, either in intermittent thrusts at a piston, or as an electric current
claims.description: A portable energy-storage substance charged electrically with wind or water power that later releases its energy to drive a piston or as electric current, like a rechargeable battery or hydrogen fuel.

claims.quote: Their advent will be the beginning of the end for steam traction on land and of the steam ship at sea: the end indeed of the Age of Coal and Steam.
claims.description: Portable energy-storage fuels will end steam locomotives and steamships and close the age of coal.

claims.quote: There can be little doubt that the sea speeds of 50 and even 60 miles an hour will be attained within the next few years.
claims.description: Ships will reach speeds of 50 to 60 miles per hour.

claims.quote: the railway carriage should not be even nine or ten feet wide, the width, that is, of the smallest room in which people can live in comfort, hung on such springs and wheels as would effectually destroy all vibration
claims.description: Railway carriages nine or ten feet wide, with suspension that removes all vibration and furnished like comfortable rooms.

claims.quote: But, as I hope to make clearer in my later papers, this "Democracy," or Wholesale method of living, like the railways, is transient—a first makeshift development of a great and finally (to me at least) quite hopeful social reorganization.
claims.description: Mass-produced, uniform ways of living, like the railways, are a passing phase that will give way to a hopeful social reorganization.

claims.quote: the happy suggestion (for the ferry transits, at any rate) of a rail along the sea bottom, which would serve as a guide to swift submarine vessels, out of reach of all that superficial "motion" that is so distressing, and of all possibilities of collision
claims.description: Fast submarine ferries guided along a rail laid on the sea floor, free of wave motion and collisions.

claims.quote: I have said nothing in this chapter, devoted to locomotion, of the coming invention of flying.
claims.description: Human flight will be invented.

claims.quote: But I do not think it at all probable that aeronautics will ever come into play as a serious modification of transport and communication—the main question here under consideration.
claims.description: Flying machines will never become a significant means of transport and communication.

claims.quote: And now, perhaps, the real significance of the previous paper, in which sea velocities of fifty miles an hour, and land travel at the rate of a hundred, and even cab and omnibus journeys of thirty or forty miles, were shown to be possible, becomes more apparent.
claims.description: Land travel at 100 miles per hour and road cab and bus trips of 30 to 40 miles become possible.

claims.quote: not only will many of these railway-begotten "giant cities" reach their maximum in the commencing century
claims.description: Today's big railway-fed cities will reach their peak size during the coming century.

claims.quote: It is much more probable that these coming cities will not be, in the old sense, cities at all; they will present a new and entirely different phase of human distribution.
claims.description: Future cities will spread out into a diffuse, low-density pattern of settlement instead of compact cities, like suburban sprawl.

claims.quote: that daily journey, that has governed and still to a very considerable extent governs the growth of cities, has had, and probably always will have, a maximum limit of two hours, one hour each way from sleeping place to council chamber, counter, workroom, or office stool
claims.description: Daily commuting will always be capped at about one hour each way, which sets the size of cities.

claims.quote: These new forces, at present still so potently centripetal in their influence, bring with them, nevertheless, the distinct promise of a centrifugal application that may be finally equal to the complete reduction of all our present congestions.
claims.description: New transport will eventually disperse city populations outward enough to end urban overcrowding.

claims.quote: And is it too much, therefore, in view of all that has been adduced in this and the previous paper, to expect that the available area for even the common daily toilers of the great city of the year 2000, or earlier, will have a radius very much larger even than that?
claims.description: By 2000 ordinary workers will commute daily from much more than 30 miles out from the city center.

claims.quote: the available area for the social equivalent of the favoured season-ticket holders of to-day will have a radius of over one hundred miles, and be almost equal to the area of Ireland
claims.description: Well-off commuters will be able to live more than 100 miles from the city where they work.

claims.quote: the London citizen of the year 2000 a.d. may have a choice of nearly all England and Wales south of Nottingham and east of Exeter as his suburb
claims.description: By 2000 a London worker could live almost anywhere in southern England and Wales as a commuter suburb.

claims.quote: the vast stretch of country from Washington to Albany will be all of it "available" to the active citizen of New York and Philadelphia before that date
claims.description: The whole region from Washington to Albany will become one commuter zone for New York and Philadelphia, a megalopolis.

claims.quote: So far as London, St. Petersburg, and Berlin go, it seems fairly safe to assume that they will go well over twenty millions; and that New York, Philadelphia, and Chicago will probably, and Hankow almost certainly, reach forty millions.
claims.description: London, St. Petersburg and Berlin will grow past 20 million people, and New York, Philadelphia, Chicago and Hankow will reach 40 million, as spread-out urban regions.

claims.quote: Even if we allowed for considerable increase in the production of food stuffs in the future, it still remains inevitable that the increase of each city in the world must come at last upon arrest.
claims.description: Every city's growth will eventually stop, capped by the trade area that sustains it.

claims.quote: And one proceeds to pack the answer in gigantic tenement houses, looming upon colossal roofed streets, provide it with moving ways (the only available transit appliances suited to such dense multitudes), and develop its manners and morals in accordance with the laws that will always prevail amidst over-crowded humanity so long as humanity endures.
claims.description: The commonly imagined future megacity of giant tenements, roofed-over streets and moving walkways, which the writer now rejects as unlikely.
